metadata.title: Understanding student performance beyond traditional factors: Evidence from PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses PISA 2012’s two-stage sampling design (schools sampled with probability proportional to size, then students sampled within schools) and therefore does not treat students as independent observations. The paper estimates standard errors using the Plausible Values (PV) methodology together with Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) using Fay’s method to account for the complex sampling variability. The dependent variable is mathematics performance represented by five plausible values per student, and all reported regression standard errors are computed under this PV+replication framework. The manuscript does not name a specific student weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly relies on PV replication methods consistent with PISA’s technical approach for unbiased standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports a robustness check where the authors restrict the sample to cases with no missing values common to the three model specifications, and they state that they assume missing values are missing randomly. However, it does not implement or report a formal missing-data imputation procedure (e.g., multiple imputation) for the main analyses, nor does it provide a complete missing-data handling protocol for the full sample beyond the restricted-sample robustness exercise. Therefore, the missing-data handling for the primary estimation is not fully specified in a way that maps to a single standard missing-data category.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2012 mathematics performance for 15-year-old students in eight Latin American economies (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Mexico, Uruguay, Peru). The dependent variable is mathematics performance represented by five plausible values per student. The paper runs multiple regression specifications (baseline with student characteristics and socioeconomic environment; traditional model adding class size and teacher certification/qualification and school type; pedagogical model adding instructional time, principal feedback, assessment use, tutoring/extra lessons, and student out-of-school additional math classes). For robustness, the authors also estimate models on a restricted sample with no missing values common to the three specifications, and they assume missingness is random to justify comparability across specifications.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Development Centre working paper analyzes associations between school inputs and students’ mathematics performance in Latin America using PISA 2012. The dependent variable is mathematics achievement represented by five plausible values per student, and standard errors are computed using the PV methodology combined with Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) with Fay’s method to reflect PISA’s two-stage sampling design. The paper estimates a baseline model with student characteristics and socioeconomic environment (ESCS for students, XESCS for schools, plus sex and age), then extends it with “traditional” school inputs (class size, teacher certification/qualification, and school type) and “pedagogical” inputs (weekly instructional time, principal feedback to teachers, use of assessment for monitoring, tutoring/extra math lessons, and students’ out-of-school additional math classes). Results indicate that student socioeconomic characteristics explain about 30% of performance variation in Latin America, and that after controlling for these, several non-traditional pedagogical inputs (notably instructional time and principal feedback, and teacher expectations) are associated with higher mathematics performance, while many traditional inputs are not consistently related. The paper also reports robustness checks using a restricted no-missing-values sample and discusses potential selection bias for some negative associations.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper that conducts econometric regression analyses on PISA 2012 mathematics achievement using plausible values and BRR/Fay replication, but it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models. Consequently, the schema’s ML-specific fields (ml_techniques and main_findings as ML target-variable performance rows) are intentionally left empty rather than fabricated. The paper’s results are presented as regression coefficients and R-squared values under PV-based estimation, which are not ML algorithm comparisons.
